passages.title: Two sons seek David's throne
passages.summary: Adonijah gathers supporters at En Rogel. Bathsheba and Nathan approach David, who orders Solomon’s anointing at Gihon.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Who speaks for Solomon when David must choose the next king?

contextNote.title: Succession requires a decision before the king dies
contextNote.text: Bathsheba names the uncertainty facing the royal household. Rival gatherings turn that uncertainty into competing public claims. Nathan's intervention brings David's authority into a process already moving without him.

passages.title: David dies and Solomon consolidates power
passages.summary: David gives final instructions. Solomon removes Abiathar and orders the deaths of Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does Solomon explain his orders against each rival?

contextNote.title: The new throne is secured through removals
contextNote.text: Solomon judges several figures through past acts and present threats. Mercy toward Abiathar still removes him from office. The chapter presents established power as a result of deliberate and sometimes deadly decisions.

passages.title: Solomon asks for wisdom and judges a dispute
passages.summary: At Gibeon, Solomon asks for an understanding heart. In Jerusalem, two women dispute the identity of a living infant.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me encourages seeking discernment between right and wrong.

contextNote.title: Wisdom begins as a request to hear people well
contextNote.text: Solomon asks for understanding needed to judge a large people. The women's dispute then tests that request in a concrete case. Royal wisdom must serve people whose household conflict reaches the court.

passages.title: Officials, provisions, and wisdom
passages.summary: The chapter lists officials, regional suppliers, royal provisions, and Solomon’s reputation for wisdom.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Who provides the food that supports Solomon’s court?

contextNote.title: Royal abundance requires a system of supply
contextNote.text: Named districts provide food for the court in monthly turns. The description of plentiful life stands beside these required contributions. The later complaint about burdens invites another view of the same royal system.

passages.title: Hiram supplies timber for the temple
passages.summary: Solomon and Hiram arrange timber and food exchanges. Adoniram supervises a labor levy, while builders prepare stone and wood.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: What does temple building require from the workers and their families?

contextNote.title: The building's beauty depends on counted labor
contextNote.text: Timber agreements alone cannot produce the temple. The chapter assigns thousands to carrying, cutting, and supervision. Read the finished building beside these workers rather than crediting its construction to Solomon alone.

passages.title: The temple is built
passages.summary: The account describes the temple’s rooms, wooden carvings, gold covering, and cherubim. God’s promise also requires faithful conduct.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites reflection on sacred space and temple symbols.

contextNote.title: A building cannot replace the duties attached to it
contextNote.text: God's speech interrupts the description of rooms and decoration. It makes continued obedience central to the promise of presence. The temple's completion does not make conduct irrelevant.

passages.title: Royal buildings and bronze furnishings
passages.summary: Solomon’s palace buildings are described. Hiram the bronze worker makes pillars, the sea, movable stands, and other vessels.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual compares the bronze sea with baptism.

contextNote.title: A temple depends on skilled workers
contextNote.text: The account names Huram’s skill before describing the bronze works. Large basins and stands require knowledge of metal and construction. Temple worship depends on labor as well as royal plans. The long description gives crafted objects a place in the story. Read that achievement beside the costs of building in chapter 5.

passages.title: The ark enters the temple and Solomon prays
passages.summary: The ark is brought into the sanctuary. Solomon prays about justice, forgiveness, drought, foreigners, war, and exile.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the dedication prayer with temple covenants and walking in God’s ways.

contextNote.title: The dedication imagines listeners beyond Israel
contextNote.text: Solomon includes a foreigner who comes to pray toward the house. He also imagines drought, defeat, and exile. The prayer assigns the temple a role beyond royal celebration and present prosperity.

passages.title: Promises, warnings, labor, and trade
passages.summary: God answers Solomon with a promise and warning. The chapter describes towns, building projects, labor, and ships sailing toward Ophir.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s promises and the responsibility to keep covenants.

contextNote.title: The warning imagines the temple as a future ruin
contextNote.text: God's answer permits the possibility that the celebrated house will become a warning. The surrounding work and trade do not cancel that danger. Visible achievement remains separate from lasting faithfulness.

passages.title: The queen of Sheba visits
passages.summary: The queen tests Solomon with questions and sees the court. Gifts, trade, gold, horses, and royal wealth follow.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: What impresses the queen besides Solomon’s wealth?

contextNote.title: A visitor's praise presents one view of courtly success
contextNote.text: The queen sees wisdom through the court's arrangements and attendants. The chapter then counts wealth, horses, and goods. Read this admired display beside the later account of subjects seeking relief.

passages.title: Solomon turns away and adversaries rise
passages.summary: Solomon supports other gods. Hadad and Rezon become adversaries. Ahijah promises Jeroboam a kingdom, and Solomon later dies.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine influences that turn their hearts from God.

contextNote.title: A divided garment makes a political warning visible
contextNote.text: Ahijah's torn garment presents the kingdom as separable portions. Solomon's worship choices now have public consequences in the account. The closing adversaries prepare the division before his son's accession.

passages.title: Rehoboam rejects the petition and the kingdom divides
passages.summary: Rehoboam rejects advice to ease the people’s burden. The northern tribes follow Jeroboam, who establishes worship at Bethel and Dan.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the effect of leaders’ choices and the need for good counsel.

contextNote.title: The divided kingdom begins with a labor complaint
contextNote.text: The people ask for relief from a heavy burden. Rehoboam treats that request as a challenge to his power. His answer breaks the kingdom he hoped to control. The split involves work, advice, and trust, not only rival leaders. Solomon’s glory has left costs that his son must answer.

passages.title: A man of God confronts Bethel
passages.summary: A man of God announces judgment at Bethel. An older prophet deceives him into eating, and a lion later kills him.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Why does the visiting prophet accept a claim that changes his earlier command?

contextNote.title: An authoritative claim can still deceive
contextNote.text: The older prophet claims an angel changed the earlier command. The account identifies that claim as a lie. Readers must distinguish what a character says from what the account establishes.

passages.title: Ahijah speaks and Shishak attacks Jerusalem
passages.summary: Jeroboam’s disguised wife visits Ahijah about their son Abijah. The child dies. The account then describes Rehoboam’s rule and Shishak’s attack.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does Ahijah’s message affect Jeroboam’s wife and child?

contextNote.title: Disguise cannot control the answer sought
contextNote.text: Jeroboam's wife arrives under a hidden identity, but Ahijah addresses her directly. The family request becomes a judgment on royal conduct. Private anxiety and public kingship meet in the same visit.

passages.title: Judah’s rulers and a new northern dynasty
passages.summary: Abijam and Asa rule Judah. Asa seeks Ben Hadad’s help against Baasha. Baasha kills Nadab and destroys Jeroboam’s household.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: What does Asa give away to gain help against Baasha?

contextNote.title: An alliance purchases relief by changing another ruler's loyalties
contextNote.text: Asa sends temple and palace treasure to Ben Hadad. The agreement answers Baasha's pressure through a neighboring king. Local security comes through resources removed from the kingdom's own stores.

passages.title: Kings fall before Omri and Ahab rise
passages.summary: Jehu condemns Baasha’s house. Zimri kills Elah and is defeated. Omri prevails over Tibni, builds Samaria, and is succeeded by Ahab.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How do the changes of kings affect their families and towns?

contextNote.title: A new capital survives rapid changes of rulers
contextNote.text: The account compresses assassinations, rival claims, and destruction of royal families. Omri's purchase and building give that unstable succession a lasting center. Ahab inherits both the city and the religious judgments surrounding his father's rule.

passages.title: Elijah and the widow at Zarephath
passages.summary: Elijah announces drought, receives food at Cherith, and stays with a widow at Zarephath. Her food endures, and her son returns to life.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the widow’s trust amid scarcity.

contextNote.title: A prophet depends on a household already facing hunger
contextNote.text: The widow describes food sufficient only for a final meal. Elijah's request places shared provision inside that scarcity. The later restoration of her son deepens the relationship beyond hospitality alone.

passages.title: Elijah confronts Ahab at Carmel
passages.summary: Obadiah meets Elijah. Elijah asks Israel to choose between God and Baal. Fire answers his prayer. Baal's prophets are killed, and rain returns.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Elijah’s challenge to examine commitment to God.

contextNote.title: A public question frames the contest as a choice
contextNote.text: Elijah challenges divided loyalty before the altar contest begins. The displayed answer therefore serves an argument already spoken. The chapter combines rain, worship, and violence rather than a harmless competition.

passages.title: Elijah receives care and calls Elisha
passages.summary: Threatened by Jezebel, Elijah flees, asks to die, receives food, and travels to Horeb. He receives renewed work and places his mantle on Elisha.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the quiet voice and Elisha’s willingness to respond.

contextNote.title: Elijah's isolation differs from the larger situation described
contextNote.text: Elijah speaks as though he alone remains faithful. God's answer names others and assigns future workers. Food and rest precede correction of both his exhaustion and his understanding.

passages.title: Ahab defeats Ben Hadad and releases him
passages.summary: Ben Hadad attacks Samaria. Prophets advise Ahab, and Israel wins two battles. Ahab releases his opponent and receives a prophetic rebuke.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Why does the prophet challenge Ahab after his victory?

contextNote.title: A victorious treaty receives a different prophetic judgment
contextNote.text: Ahab treats release and trade rights as a successful agreement. The prophet judges that settlement through a duty Ahab did not fulfill. Military success does not settle the account's evaluation of kingship.

passages.title: Naboth is killed and Elijah confronts Ahab
passages.summary: Naboth refuses to give up his vineyard. Jezebel arranges false accusations and his killing. Ahab takes possession, and Elijah announces judgment.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How do Ahab and Jezebel use their power against Naboth? What does Elijah say about their actions?

contextNote.title: An inherited field is more than a commodity
contextNote.text: Naboth refuses because the vineyard belongs to his family’s inheritance. Ahab sees useful land beside his palace. Jezebel uses public charges and witnesses to remove the owner. The court turns law into a means of theft. Elijah’s judgment connects the royal household with that misuse of power.

passages.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
passages.summary: Ahab and Jehoshaphat seek counsel about Ramoth Gilead. Micaiah describes a heavenly council and predicts defeat. Ahab dies in battle.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual reads the lying spirit as God allowing deception.

contextNote.title: The court pressures a speaker to match an approved answer
contextNote.text: The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the favorable predictions. Micaiah refuses to make agreement his measure of truth. The council scene exposes the risks of asking questions while controlling acceptable answers.

events.summary: Elijah announces drought, receives food at Cherith, and stays with a widow at Zarephath. Her food endures, and her son returns to life.
events.detail: The widow describes food sufficient only for a final meal. Elijah's request places shared provision inside that scarcity. The later restoration of her son deepens the relationship beyond hospitality alone.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the widow’s trust amid scarcity.

events.title: Elijah confronts Ahab at Carmel
events.summary: Obadiah meets Elijah. Elijah asks Israel to choose between God and Baal. Fire answers his prayer. Baal's prophets are killed, and rain returns.
events.detail: Elijah challenges divided loyalty before the altar contest begins. The displayed answer therefore serves an argument already spoken. The chapter combines rain, worship, and violence rather than a harmless competition.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Elijah’s challenge to examine commitment to God.

events.title: Elijah receives care and calls Elisha
events.summary: Threatened by Jezebel, Elijah flees, asks to die, receives food, and travels to Horeb. He receives renewed work and places his mantle on Elisha.
events.detail: Elijah speaks as though he alone remains faithful. God's answer names others and assigns future workers. Food and rest precede correction of both his exhaustion and his understanding.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the quiet voice and Elisha’s willingness to respond.

events.title: Ahab defeats Ben Hadad and releases him
events.summary: Ben Hadad attacks Samaria. Prophets advise Ahab, and Israel wins two battles. Ahab releases his opponent and receives a prophetic rebuke.
events.detail: Ahab treats release and trade rights as a successful agreement. The prophet judges that settlement through a duty Ahab did not fulfill. Military success does not settle the account's evaluation of kingship.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Why does the prophet challenge Ahab after his victory?

events.title: Naboth is killed and Elijah confronts Ahab
events.summary: Naboth refuses to give up his vineyard. Jezebel arranges false accusations and his killing. Ahab takes possession, and Elijah announces judgment.
events.detail: Naboth refuses because the vineyard belongs to his family’s inheritance. Ahab sees useful land beside his palace. Jezebel uses public charges and witnesses to remove the owner. The court turns law into a means of theft. Elijah’s judgment connects the royal household with that misuse of power.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How do Ahab and Jezebel use their power against Naboth? What does Elijah say about their actions?

events.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
events.summary: Ahab and Jehoshaphat seek counsel about Ramoth Gilead. Micaiah describes a heavenly council and predicts defeat. Ahab dies in battle.
events.detail: The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the favorable predictions. Micaiah refuses to make agreement his measure of truth. The council scene exposes the risks of asking questions while controlling acceptable answers.

guides.title: 1 Kings: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A temple depends on skilled workers
steps.text: The account names Huram’s skill before describing the bronze works. Large basins and stands require knowledge of metal and construction. Temple worship depends on labor as well as royal plans. The long description gives crafted objects a place in the story. Read that achievement beside the costs of building in chapter 5.

steps.title: The divided kingdom begins with a labor complaint
steps.text: The people ask for relief from a heavy burden. Rehoboam treats that request as a challenge to his power. His answer breaks the kingdom he hoped to control. The split involves work, advice, and trust, not only rival leaders. Solomon’s glory has left costs that his son must answer.

steps.title: An inherited field is more than a commodity
steps.text: Naboth refuses because the vineyard belongs to his family’s inheritance. Ahab sees useful land beside his palace. Jezebel uses public charges and witnesses to remove the owner. The court turns law into a means of theft. Elijah’s judgment connects the royal household with that misuse of power.

textRoutes.title: Two sons seek David's throne
textRoutes.summary: Adonijah gathers supporters at En Rogel. Bathsheba and Nathan approach David, who orders Solomon’s anointing at Gihon.
textRoutes.detail: Bathsheba names the uncertainty facing the royal household. Rival gatherings turn that uncertainty into competing public claims. Nathan's intervention brings David's authority into a process already moving without him.

textRoutes.title: David dies and Solomon consolidates power
textRoutes.summary: David gives final instructions. Solomon removes Abiathar and orders the deaths of Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei.
textRoutes.detail: Solomon judges several figures through past acts and present threats. Mercy toward Abiathar still removes him from office. The chapter presents established power as a result of deliberate and sometimes deadly decisions.

textRoutes.title: Hiram supplies timber for the temple
textRoutes.summary: Solomon and Hiram arrange timber and food exchanges. Adoniram supervises a labor levy, while builders prepare stone and wood.
textRoutes.detail: Timber agreements alone cannot produce the temple. The chapter assigns thousands to carrying, cutting, and supervision. Read the finished building beside these workers rather than crediting its construction to Solomon alone.

textRoutes.title: Solomon turns away and adversaries rise
textRoutes.summary: Solomon supports other gods. Hadad and Rezon become adversaries. Ahijah promises Jeroboam a kingdom, and Solomon later dies.
textRoutes.detail: Ahijah's torn garment presents the kingdom as separable portions. Solomon's worship choices now have public consequences in the account. The closing adversaries prepare the division before his son's accession.

textRoutes.title: Rehoboam rejects the petition and the kingdom divides
textRoutes.summary: Rehoboam rejects advice to ease the people’s burden. The northern tribes follow Jeroboam, who establishes worship at Bethel and Dan.
textRoutes.detail: The people ask for relief from a heavy burden. Rehoboam treats that request as a challenge to his power. His answer breaks the kingdom he hoped to control. The split involves work, advice, and trust, not only rival leaders. Solomon’s glory has left costs that his son must answer.

textRoutes.title: Ahijah speaks and Shishak attacks Jerusalem
textRoutes.summary: Jeroboam’s disguised wife visits Ahijah about their son Abijah. The child dies. The account then describes Rehoboam’s rule and Shishak’s attack.
textRoutes.detail: Jeroboam's wife arrives under a hidden identity, but Ahijah addresses her directly. The family request becomes a judgment on royal conduct. Private anxiety and public kingship meet in the same visit.

textRoutes.title: Elijah and the widow at Zarephath
textRoutes.summary: Elijah announces drought, receives food at Cherith, and stays with a widow at Zarephath. Her food endures, and her son returns to life.
textRoutes.detail: The widow describes food sufficient only for a final meal. Elijah's request places shared provision inside that scarcity. The later restoration of her son deepens the relationship beyond hospitality alone.

textRoutes.title: Elijah confronts Ahab at Carmel
textRoutes.summary: Obadiah meets Elijah. Elijah asks Israel to choose between God and Baal. Fire answers his prayer. Baal's prophets are killed, and rain returns.
textRoutes.detail: Elijah challenges divided loyalty before the altar contest begins. The displayed answer therefore serves an argument already spoken. The chapter combines rain, worship, and violence rather than a harmless competition.

textRoutes.title: Elijah receives care and calls Elisha
textRoutes.summary: Threatened by Jezebel, Elijah flees, asks to die, receives food, and travels to Horeb. He receives renewed work and places his mantle on Elisha.
textRoutes.detail: Elijah speaks as though he alone remains faithful. God's answer names others and assigns future workers. Food and rest precede correction of both his exhaustion and his understanding.

textRoutes.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
textRoutes.summary: Ahab and Jehoshaphat seek counsel about Ramoth Gilead. Micaiah describes a heavenly council and predicts defeat. Ahab dies in battle.
textRoutes.detail: The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the favorable predictions. Micaiah refuses to make agreement his measure of truth. The council scene exposes the risks of asking questions while controlling acceptable answers.
